title: Sent Home from the Battle
summary: The Philistine armies muster at Aphek, and David and his men march at the rear with Achish. The other Philistine commanders object, fearing that David will turn on them in battle to win back Saul's favor. Achish, protesting that he has found no fault in David, sends him back to Ziklag, and the Philistines go up to Jezreel without him.
story: Chapter 28 left David in an impossible position: he had agreed to march with the Philistines against Israel. If he fought, he would be killing his own people and fighting the anointed king he had twice refused to harm; if he refused or turned in battle, his cover would be blown and his men endangered. This chapter resolves the dilemma without David lifting a finger. The suspicion of the Philistine commanders, not any plan of David's, removes him from the battlefield. The narrator steps back in time to do it: the Philistines are still gathering at Aphek, before they move to Shunem (28:4). The chapter also sets up the next one, because the three days David spends marching home are the days in which the Amalekites burn Ziklag.
historical:
Aphek, at the southern edge of the Sharon plain near the source of the Yarkon River, was a natural mustering point for Philistine forces heading north along the coastal route. The Philistines had gathered there before the battle in which the ark was captured (1 Samuel 4:1). From Aphek the road ran north and then east into the Jezreel Valley, where Saul waited by the spring in Jezreel at the foot of Gilboa.

The Philistines were a coalition of five city-states, each with its own ruler, and the chapter shows how that coalition worked. Achish, though David's patron, cannot overrule the other commanders; the army moves by consensus among its leaders. Their fear was grounded in experience. Earlier in Saul's reign, Hebrews who had been serving with the Philistines went over to Israel in the middle of a battle (14:21). A band of six hundred Hebrew fighters at the rear of the Philistine army was exactly the kind of risk no commander would want.
cultural:
The Philistine commanders call David and his men Hebrews, the term foreigners in the Old Testament often use for Israelites. It marks them as outsiders whose loyalties lie elsewhere. They quote the victory song the women of Israel sang after David killed Goliath, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands” (compare 18:7 and 21:11). The song had made Saul jealous; now it makes the Philistines wary. David's reputation, built by killing Philistines, follows him even into their camp.

Achish's language is remarkable for a Philistine king. He swears, “As surely as the LORD lives”, using the name of Israel's God, perhaps as a courtesy to David, and he compares David to an angel of God, a phrase later used by others to flatter David as king (2 Samuel 14:17 and 19:27). The idea behind the heads of our men in verse 4 is grimly practical: a soldier returning to his master with enemy heads proves his loyalty in the most visible way possible, as David himself once brought Goliath's head to Saul.
literary: The chapter is almost entirely dialogue, and it runs on irony. Achish praises David's loyalty in strong terms three times (verses 3, 6, and 9), yet the reader knows from chapter 27 that David has been deceiving him the whole time. The commanders, whom Achish thinks unfair, are the only ones who judge the situation correctly. David's protest in verse 8 is a masterpiece of ambiguity. He asks why he cannot go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king. Achish hears himself as the lord the king, but Israel's king is Saul, and the words could just as well mean that David wants to fight the Philistines. The narrator never tells us what David intended. The key point is that God, working through Philistine suspicion, gets David out of the trap.

outline.t: The Philistines muster at Aphek with David at the rear
David returns; the Philistines go up to Jezreel

doctrines.note: God delivers David from an impossible situation through the ordinary suspicions of his enemies. The chapter never mentions God acting, but the whole outcome shows his hand: David is kept from fighting Israel and from any part in Saul's death, which will matter greatly when he becomes king.

The rulers of the Philistines make their decision for their own reasons, yet it serves the LORD's purpose for David. Scripture often shows God directing the choices of those who do not know him without overriding them.

words.note: Satan, adversary or opponent. Here it is used of a human enemy: the commanders fear David will become their adversary in battle. The word is used this way elsewhere of human opponents (for example 1 Kings 11:14). Only later in the Old Testament does it become a title for a heavenly accuser, and later still the proper name Satan. This chapter shows the word's everyday meaning.

Malak, messenger, used both for human envoys and for angels, the messengers of God. When Achish says David is as pleasing to him as an angel of God, he means a figure of perfect goodness and wisdom. The compliment is sincere and misplaced, since David has been lying to him.

Yashar, upright or straight. Achish calls David upright in his sight. The word is a common term of moral praise in Scripture (for example, people doing what was right in their own eyes in Judges, using the same root). The qualifier in my sight matters: Achish's judgment is based on appearances he has been given.

christ: The chapter holds no prediction of Christ. Its link to the larger story is God's protection of the anointed king's integrity. David must not be the one who brings down Saul, and the LORD sees to it that he is miles away when Saul falls. In the New Testament, God likewise guards the purposes bound up in his chosen king, and Jesus repeatedly slips away from danger until his hour has come (John 7:30, 8:59). The connection is a pattern of God's care for his anointed and his timing, not an allegory hidden in the text.
questions: David was rescued from a problem of his own making by circumstances he did not control. Can you recognize times when God closed a door that you were about to walk through unwisely?
Achish trusted appearances, and the commanders judged by reputation. What do you rely on when deciding whom to trust?
David's reputation followed him everywhere he went. What reputation follows you, and what has built it?
